topic.title: How Motorola's team built the first handheld mobile phone in six weeks for a 1973 demo, then took ten more years to sell one

title: Why Was the First Mobile Phone a Brick?
description:
Why was the first phone you could carry, Motorola's, the size of a brick?
We build the 1973 prototype part by part in 3D, follow it to the street demo in New York, then stand the first phone you could buy beside the one in your hand.
Sources: Motorola Solutions, Guinness World Records (Nov 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.
cta: What should we build in 3D next? Comment

lines.text: Motorola's first phone you could carry was a brick. Why?
Its engineers had just 6 weeks to build one, to show America's phone regulators.
Everything had to fit in one hand: a radio, an antenna, and a battery to power them.
How does it call with no wire? The radio turns your voice into radio waves for a tower nearby.
Each tower covers one small patch, a cell. That's the cell in cell phone.
In April of 1973 it made a real call, on a New York street.
But that phone wasn't for sale. The first one you could buy weighed 785 grams, and was 300 millimetres long.
Getting that brick into a shop took over $100M of Motorola's money, and more than 10 years.
All of that, for a phone that fit in one hand.
